title: Tenali Raman and the Miserly Brahmin's Last Coin
summary: In a quiet ward of Vijayanagara lived an old scholar named Somayaji, who had accumulated two thousand gold coins through a lifetime of extreme frugality. He wore threadbare rags...
full_text:
In a quiet ward of Vijayanagara lived an old scholar named Somayaji, who had accumulated two thousand gold coins through a lifetime of extreme frugality. He wore threadbare rags, ate only dry rice crusts, starved his family, and refused to spend a single copper on doctor's medicine when sick.
Every midnight, he would unearth an iron pot buried beneath his bedroom floor, count his gold coins, weep with greedy joy, and bury them again.

One night, a clever burglar observed him through a window crack, dug up the iron pot while Somayaji was asleep, and vanished with all the gold!

The next morning, when Somayaji found the empty hole in the floor, he collapsed in agonizing despair. He tore his hair, beat his chest, and screamed so loudly that the entire neighborhood gathered:
'My gold is gone! My life is over! I will drown myself in the well!'

Tenali Raman arrived at the scene.
He looked at the empty pit, picked up a large, heavy granite river stone from the courtyard, and dropped it into the hole:
*THUD!*

Tenali turned to the weeping miser:
'Somayaji, dry your tears. Cover this stone with earth, and pretend it is your pot of gold!'

Somayaji yelled in fury:
'Tenali, art thou mocking my ruin? A granite stone is not a pot of gold! I cannot spend a stone!'

Tenali Raman looked at him with profound philosophical clarity:
'Didst thou ever spend a single copper of thy gold while it was buried in that hole?
Didst thou buy clothes to warm thy shivering back?
Didst thou buy medicine to heal thy cough?
Didst thou share a grain of rice with a starving child?
No!
Thou didst only look at it in the dark, touch it, and bury it in the dirt!
For twenty years, thy gold was nothing more than heavy stones resting in the mud!
Cover this stone with earth, look at the spot every midnight, and imagine thy gold is still there!
For gold that is never spent, never shared, and never used to relieve human suffering has no more value than common granite dirt!'

The crowd murmured in deep approval of Tenali’s profound words.
Somayaji stood transfixed. The truth pierced through his hardened heart of avarice like an arrow of light.
He realized that his greed had made him a penniless beggar while sitting upon a fortune.
When the police recovered half his stolen gold a week later, Somayaji was a transformed man: he built a hospital ward for the poor, bought warm clothes for his family, and lived with generous peace, cured of his miserly blindness forever.
moral: A hoarder who loves money more than life discovers that unspent gold buried in dirt is no different from common stones.
